Stale index entry: Workspaces land on desktop

Stale index text about workspaces that the reader navigated away from. Workspaces group the projects you keep returning to, and remember the layout you left them in. This copy is still mounted because the router keeps the previous route around, and it must never be read aloud.

More stale index text, this time about syncing. Every workspace now syncs in the background, which means the version you open on a second machine is the version you left behind on the first one, down to the scroll position of each open file.

Stale index entry: Search gets a query language

Stale index text about search. The new query language understands fields, ranges and negation, so a search can be narrowed to one author, one directory and one week without leaving the search box or learning a second tool.

Stale index text about indexing. Results now stream in as the index is walked, so the first matches appear immediately instead of after the whole repository has been scanned.

Stale index entry: Review comments become threads

Stale index text about review threads. A comment on a line now opens a thread that travels with the line as the file is edited, so a question asked on Monday still points at the right code on Thursday.

Stale index text about notifications. Replies arrive as one digest per thread rather than one message per reply, which keeps a long argument from filling an inbox.

Stale index entry: Terminals remember their working directory

Stale index text about terminals. A terminal reopened in a project now starts where it left off, in the directory you were last working in, with the scrollback from the previous session still available above the prompt.

Stale index text about shells. The shell integration no longer depends on editing a profile script, which means a terminal behaves the same on a fresh machine as it does on one that has been configured for years.

Stale index entry: Settings move into the project

Stale index text about settings. Anything that affects how a project builds or runs can now be committed alongside it, so a new contributor inherits a working configuration instead of a paragraph in a readme describing one.

Stale index text about precedence. Personal preferences still win over project settings for anything cosmetic, and lose for anything that would change the output of a build.

Sep 23, 2026 · Changelog

Shipping rollouts and review

Today we are launching two assistants for the last mile of shipping code. The first watches every change as it deploys and reports its health per environment. The second reports exploitable bugs on every pull request, before a human reviewer has to find them.

Both are available today on team and enterprise plans.

Rollouts

Rollouts attaches a monitor to every pull request and watches the change as it deploys, reporting change health per environment: verified healthy, regression detected, or inconclusive. Enable it from the dashboard and connect source control, your deploy system and your telemetry provider.

Monitoring plans

When a pull request opens, the monitor reads the diff and the systems it touches, then writes a monitoring plan as a comment. The plan lists the risks it identified, the effect the change is meant to have, the signals it will check, and any gaps in instrumentation that would make the change hard to verify. Edit the plan and the monitor uses your version.

Deploy tracking

Each deployment is tracked from the moment it starts rolling until the signals settle, so a regression that only appears under production load is still attributed to the change that caused it rather than to whatever happened to deploy next.

Security review

Security review reads a pull request the way an attacker would, looking for the bugs that can actually be reached from outside: injection through an unvalidated parameter, a missing authorization check on a new route, a secret that escapes into a log line.

It reports only what it can argue is exploitable, with the path from the entry point to the vulnerable line, so a reviewer can judge the finding instead of triaging a list.

Configuration lives next to the rest of your automation:

rollouts:
  environments: [staging, production]
  telemetry: provider-of-choice

Hidden paragraph that is present in the markup but not rendered, and must never be read.

Both assistants are off by default. Turn them on per repository, and turn them off again from the same screen if they are not pulling their weight.
